articles.headline: Funny numbers
articles.dek: OpenAI’s revenue mix-up, and the dotcom habit of inventing metrics

blocks.text: I started my career in the dotcom bubble, and the dotcom bubble had a lot of funny numbers. There were metrics that people didn’t really understand or didn’t mean much, like ‘hits’, bandwidth or the number of hosts on the internet. There were also carefully created new ‘adjusted’ metrics that avoided all the stuff you didn’t want to talk about. My personal favourite was the new entrant mobile operator that started talking to investors about EBITDA before customer acquisition: the main costs for the business were capex and customer acquisition, so ‘EBITDA before CAC’ was effectively ‘revenue’. There were a bunch of jokes at the time about how the next metric would be ‘earnings before costs’.
We’re seeing a lot of the same stuff this time around. We don’t really know what metrics would be best, we don’t have the metrics that we would like anyway, and the metrics we do have are… funny.
OpenAI’s revenue number

Late last month, Axios and other media outlets reported that OpenAI’s annualised monthly revenue had passed $70bn. This week, it emerged that this was a mistake and the actual number was ‘close to $50bn’. The confusion seems to be that in general OpenAI has been reporting revenue net of payments to companies that resell its models (Microsoft, AWS) where Anthropic has been reporting gross, and both OpenAI and investors were also trying to gross-up the numbers to make them comparable, without making it clear which numbers they were using when leaking to the media.

articles.headline: A Landmark Study of Our Immune System Aging With A Promising Blood Test
articles.dek: A Tale of Two T Cells: GZMK+ vs GZMB+ memory cells and what they mean for healthspan

blocks.alt: Schematic of CD8+ effector-memory T cells with GZMB-rich and GZMK-rich granules
blocks.caption: Schematic figure made with the help of ChatGPT

blocks.text: In the journal Immunity a paper with an obscure title was published on October 9th, 2026. It was entitled “Single-cell analyses of global cohorts outline determinants of immune aging and link the ratio of GZMK+ to GZMB+ Tem cells to health trajectories,” which I think is one of the worst titles I have ever seen for, ironically, one of the most important papers in the science of aging. I still don’t understand why authors and journal editors use or allow such arcane titles!

In this edition of Ground Truths I’m going to unpack the extraordinary work done by the team led by Maxim Artyomov. It takes our understanding of how our immune system ages—both healthily and unhealthily—to a new level with practical implications for determining its status, and promoting our healthspan.
This turns out to be a tale of two cells—different subtypes of memory T cells—that contain distinct types of granules resulting in divergent functions. And, importantly, major health outcomes.
Phase 1: Massive Single-Cell RNA Sequencing
Some very impressive stats for who was studied and what was done:
—8 international cohorts, 2,609 individuals, 12,394,834 white blood cells
—age 18 to 98 years
—59 immune cell types from sc-RNA seq harmonization

The story starts with the thymus gland, which starts to involute in early life and accelerates after puberty, after which there is progressive loss of naive T cells and recent thymic emigrants (RTEs) with age. This decline was the strongest predictor of chronological age in the study. The problem is not so much that the naive T cells, the “rookies,” are declining but what is coming in, as the immune system adapts, to replace them—the “veterans.”

Until this study, prior cell sorting (flow cytometry) or pooled sequencing methods could not differentiate CD8+ effector memory T cells. That was only enabled by obtaining single-cell transcriptomes at scale.

The 2 types of veterans are effector memory T cells (Tem) that are either mainly granzyme K or B. You can think of the B as “bad,” since these cells are leaky, exhausted, and spilling of their granules leads to dissolution of matrix, disruption of tissue, activation of macrophages, and inflammation. That profile of the terminally differentiated GZMB+ cells was characterized from experiments in mice. The bifurcation (Figure below) is influenced towards GZMB+ by cytomegalovirus (CMV) exposure and chronic diseases, such as cardiovascular (CVD) or metabolic (such as Type 2 diabetes).

blocks.alt: Diagram of the two paths naive T cells can take as they become veteran memory T cells
blocks.caption: The 2 paths that the naive T cells can differentiate to as the rookies become veterans. The path to GZMB+ is influenced by CMV and chronic diseases. Figure made with a combination of Google Gemini and ChatGPT.

blocks.text: Phase 2: High-Throughput Proteomics

Doing single-cell RNA seq at scale to correlate with clinical outcomes or for development of a clinically useful blood test is not practical, not to mention expensive. Instead, using the Olink assay of thousands of plasma proteins in 4 independent cohorts (of the 8 used in Phase 1) per cent TemB+ (Tem stands for T effector memory cell) correlated the best with the single cell GZMB+ data (using a LASSO computational model). That protein signature was tightly correlated with the single-cell RNA-seq work, as seen below in each of the 4 cohorts.
Note: Throughout this post please recognize the interchangeability of terms established between GZMB+ and TemB+, or GZMK+ and TemK+.

blocks.alt: Scatter plots of predicted % Tem GZMB+ from Olink protein data versus single-cell measurements across four cohorts

blocks.text: Then TemB+ was validated for clinical outcomes in the UK Biobank in 48,620 participants with 17-year follow-up, using both the cell protein data. As you can see below, individuals with a high per cent TemB+ had a much higher all-cause mortality than those with low % Tem B+ or the average group, as categorized in tertiles. The x-axis is years of follow-up.

blocks.alt: Chart of all-cause mortality over 17 years for high, average and low % TemB+ groups
blocks.caption: Figure made with help of Google Gemini

blocks.text: The TemB+ % was predictive of multiple specific health outcomes as shown below. In contrast, however, note the lack of any predictive correlation with neurodegenerative diseases and macular degeneration: Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease, dementia, and age-related macular degeneration.

blocks.alt: Panels showing disease incidence by % TemB+ for several diseases, and diseases where it is not predictive

blocks.text: To emphasize the contribution of viral exposure and inflammation, the people who were seropositive for CMV had higher GZMB+ and those with higher C-reactive protein had higher % TemB+.

blocks.alt: Plots of predicted % TemB+ by CMV and EBV infection status and by C-reactive protein group

blocks.text: Here is a simplified dichotomy of clinical outcomes and inflammaging based on high Tem B+% (or GZMB+).

blocks.alt: Healthy aging (high GZMK+, low GZMB+) versus disease-associated aging (low GZMK+, high GZMB+)
blocks.caption: Figure made with help from Google Gemini

blocks.text: Of course there are plenty of limitations. The patients in the multiple cohorts were predominantly of European and Asian ancestry, leaving some uncertainty as to whether the findings will extrapolate to those of African ancestry. The window into immune cell aging was purely via blood cells, not tissue. TemB+ was measured at a single time point, so we don’t know how it changes within a person, or whether lowering it changes the risk. Importantly, the dichotomy of the “good” and “bad” TemK+ and TemB+ cells, respectively, is an over-simplification, since we know K cell granules can also promote inflammation. CD8+ T cell counts weren’t available in the UK Biobank so they had to be imputed with a model. None of this work is establishing causality. I have not gotten into the “weeds” of the report, which is a beast to read and unravel, and there is much more about different types of cells, other mouse experimental data, Type 2 immunity remodeling, and so on.
Implications

This is a seminal paper, the most comprehensive assessment of white blood cells across the human lifespan that tracks immune cell aging and its relationship with survival and multiple adverse health outcomes. Let me break it down to the key points:
Primacy of the thymus gland. The study identified the decline in naive T cells and recent thymic emigrants as the basis of the aging clock, predicting chronological age.

It’s not just that we lose naive T cells as the thymus involutes, but it’s about the type of cells that come in to replace them. And it turns out there’s a critical bifurcation between TemK+ and TemB+ cells. The difference in the granules of these cells can account for inciting or fostering inflammation. Extensive characterization of the TemB+ cells from mice showed their propensity to be leaky, exhausted, and tissue disruptive.

Viral exposure, most notably by CMV blood positivity, affects the bifurcation path to promote TemB+ cells. The other main influence on promoting TemB+ instead of TemK+ were chronic diseases, notably cardiovascular and metabolic.

The discovery in the work using single-cell RNA sequencing in >12 million white blood cells of the bifurcation and link to outcomes might not have been made with traditional methodologies of cell sorting, flow cytometry, or pooled sequencing. This is yet another reinforcement of getting “granular” (no pun intended with granules) with respect to learning from single-cell data.

A new protein blood test emerges from this body of work, the percent of TemB+, or ratio of TemB+ to TemK+. It might be considered a master indicator of unfavorable immune system aging. This could lead to a simple and inexpensive window into a person’s immune status and the researchers in the current study are indeed pursuing that goal. For people found to have an unfavorable immune status, we know of ways that can be improved with lifestyle factors and vaccines, and much more will be done in the years ahead to find other means.

Here in late 2026 we have no way of assessing a person’s immune system in the clinic, as I’ve previously written on “Why We Need an Immunome.” Ironically, we have so many ways to control the immune system, releasing its brakes (think immune checkpoint inhibitors and ten other classes of interventions) and B-cell depletion or “inverse” vaccines to induce tolerance in autoimmune conditions. We can dial it up or down but can’t measure it!

In recent months we have seen 2 new practical ways to get at this crucial assessment: (1) AI analysis of the thymus gland from a low resolution chest CT (See “Your Thymus and Your Healthspan”) and (2) Proteomic clocks of the immune system and immune cells (see “Medicine is Moving from Calendars to Clocks”) from a blood test. Both these immune system assessments are now moving towards commercial availability. The current study represents a 3rd path. In short, we’re getting there!

NB. I wrote this post. I did use AI to generate four of the Figures as noted above to help the reader visualize what I was writing about. I have no conflicts of interest related to this topic or post.

articles.headline: Agent incentives, open models outside China and an IPO overhang
articles.dek: Benedict’s Newsletter No. 664: who gets to own the customer when agents do the shopping

blocks.text: Agent incentives

Agents remain super hot, even if Muse and especially Instinct look an awful lot like the fever-brain excitement around Clubhouse in the pandemic. But if they are going to work, lots of other things need to be plugged together, most obviously how they actually talk to other websites and each other. Meta has launched a new standard (‘Personal Agent Protocol’) with the bunch of logos on the slide. Standards, of course, are one of the key strategic weapons when tech ecosystems try to go to war, and it’s always notable who isn’t on the list, and important to remember that getting the partnership person to sign a partnership deal is not the same as getting the company to use the partnership.

Meanwhile, Amazon and a bunch of other retailers are blocking agents entirely. This is partly short-term concern around fraud chargebacks and liability, and it’s not irrational for them to press pause until they worked out how to manage this more generally. There’s a 20-year-old and 150-year-old question of customer ownership versus distribution. If you’re big and already have traffic, you want to own the experience and talk to the customer directly, and if you’re small, you’re willing to take distribution instead. The additional wrinkle, of course, is that Amazon did $75 billion of ad revenue in the last 12 months, and the agent doesn’t see the ads.
Open outside China

Since Meta abandoned Llama, most of the credible open source models have come from China, which skews the debate about open a fair bit, but now American startup Reflection has launched a pretty credible open model and Mistral, which everyone had forgotten about, has come back from France with a credible model of its own. The FT reports that Nvidia is looking at buying Reflection, as part of the Bank of Jensen strategy to accelerate AI adoption while fragmenting the customer base.
IPO overhang

I think there were two fundamental changes in AI this year: agentic coding achieved explosive product-market fit, and AI infrastructure capex outgrew the cash flows of the hyperscalers and had to go to the financial markets. There’s been an enormous amount of capital raising of every kind this year, and markets are starting to get uncomfortable: in the last quarter a whole bunch of IPOs were pulled, partly also due to the imminent Anthropic IPO crowding everything out.

articles.headline: Michael Lewis: The NIH “Murder Mystery,” DOGE, and Our Government Immune System
articles.dek: Eric Topol’s conversation with Michael Lewis on his new book Blockers (63 min video)

blocks.alt: Cover of Michael Lewis’s book Blockers

blocks.text: Michael Lewis is one of, if not the best storyteller of our era. You know and likely have read his books Moneyball, The Big Short, The Blind Side, Flash Boys, Liar’s Poker, and The Undoing Project, to name a few. He has long been one of my favorite authors.

This was the first interview that Michael did on his new book, Blockers, published on October 6th, streamed live on Substack Sept 29th. It’s his 21st book and 4 of the last 5 have been about the US government: The Fifth Risk (2019), Premonition (2021), and Who Is Government? (2025).

His ability to talk with the silent civil servant heroes of multiple government agencies (the Blockers), members of the DOGE destruction team, and much more from the current US government administration.

blocks.alt: Excerpt page: Michael Lewis on the lone security guard who resisted DOGE
blocks.caption: Exclusive excerpt from Blockers in the Wall Street Journal

blocks.text: I won’t review all the things we discussed here, but the chapter on the NIH reads like an Agatha Christie murder mystery. We learned a whole different version of what happened that differed from what was previously reported.
Thank you to the nearly 500 viewers who tuned in to the live video with Michael Lewis!

articles.headline: The week in AI, SpaceX Mobile and Apple as shadow ads regulator
articles.dek: Plus ideas, outside interests and data from Benedict’s Newsletter No. 664

blocks.text: The week in AI

Anthropic quietly updated its terms and conditions to say you’re not allowed to be “cruel” to its models. This is more of the anthropomorphism that seems like sensible speculation at a minimum to some AI researchers and insane to a lot of other people, as I wrote in my column last week. Meanwhile, it creates circularity problems - if you tell a model it has X characteristic, it will try to look like that.

OpenAI followed Anthropic in building a text watermarking system to comply with EU requirements. Unlike Anthropic, this is only applied in the EU, and OpenAI is also a lot clearer that they don’t think this is really a good idea: the tech is not reliable enough and too easy to work-around.

Google launched Playground, an experimental space to use AI to generate your own games. AI is clearly going to transform both the economics of creating games (especially the hugely-expensive content creation of AAA games) and the mechanics of how games work (the NPCs can actually be intelligent now), as well as letting people spin-up improvised games like this. Compare mobile and app stores, and 3D.

Google launched a native Mac app that can connect to all of your software and take notes on what you’re working on, all running locally on-device. I don’t think it’s clear yet whether things like this are a feature or product, but meanwhile it is both predictable and hilarious that this looks nothing like a native Mac app, the download link doesn’t work in Safari, and the app is called “Google AI Edge Foresight”, which is exactly how Microsoft names products.
SpaceX Mobile

Following its earlier comments, SpaceX bought a portfolio of low-frequency cellular spectrum in the USA that would be needed to build an actual terrestrial network. US mobile operator stocks fell sharply. As I’ve I pointed out before, while SpaceX technology is extremely cool, satellite is either impractical or useless for the vast majority of real cellular use, and so if SpaceX actually wants to build a US mobile service, it will have to build what everyone else has built, spend more or less what anybody else would spend, charge more or less the same prices, and provide probably a mostly inferior service (the best sites are already taken). The most cynical interpretations remain that this is really leverage to get a good MVNO deal.
Apple as shadow ads regulator

Last month Apple briefly blocked one of the big ad network domains on iOS, and now there’s a wave of speculation that it’s working on a blacklist of a huge number of third-party targeting services, all of which allow advertisers to do terrible evil anti-democratic things to violate your human rights, like show you products you might be interested in and make money for independent publishers.

Apple here is an interesting example of what’s sometimes called a shadow regulator: it’s doing things that are really public policy rather than engineering or product decisions, but doing them without any due process, accountability or debate on devices used by well over half of Americans.
Ideas

A reminder to people who want to argue about whether LLMs could ever be conscious: our understanding of what consciousness really is remains so limited that we don’t even know if infants are conscious.

An interesting piece by cryptographer Matthew Green on the history of law enforcement access to messages and encryption and how the coming wave of AI bug fixing might mean that law enforcement will no longer be able to hack your iPhone to get your messages and their visibility on criminal and terrorist comms will go dark.
Satya Nadella wrote on his personal blog about liability when agents go wrong.
Outside interests
Christie’s is selling something very small and very beautiful.

Early next year, Bonham’s will be selling a selection of items from Stanley Kubrick’s estate. In the preview, they show a prop axe from The Shining - the axe that Jack Nicholson used on Scatman Crothers - and also the Grady twins’ dresses.
Data
Gallup has an update on global sentiment towards AI - as ever, it is inversely proportionate to national income.
PC shipments are down 20% year on year as the AI semiconductor crunch drives up pricing.
